venue_now: Not shown in the text: the file is arXiv:2310.07018v1, 10 Oct 2023 (p.1). cited_set_resolution.md lists Findings of EMNLP 2023, pp. 9743-9758.
what_it_is: A repository, generation pipeline and benchmark for LLMs' physical reasoning about everyday objects (p.1). Crowd workers rated 700+ household objects on eight attributes (elasticity, stiffness, brittleness, malleability, softness, sharpness, surface smoothness, surface hardness) on a 3-point scale, with at least four annotators per pair, giving 20,000+ annotations filtered at 0.75 agreement into 2,800 object-attribute pairs (pp.1-3). Question templates are filled from the repository to generate questions; the released benchmark has 160K multiple-choice and Boolean questions in three tracks: attribute comprehension, explicit application and implicit scenario-based analysis (pp.3-4). Ten models are scored by agreement with the human majority or by accuracy; GPT-4 is less consistent than humans on object attributes (50% vs 84%) but averages 87.7% on the scenario track (p.1, p.6).
domain: commonsense physical reasoning about attributes of everyday objects (qualitative, not numerical) (pp.1-2)
size: 2,800 object-attribute pairs over 700+ objects and 8 attributes; 160K pre-generated questions; 10 language models in the main tables plus BERT fine-tuning experiments (pp.1-6)
source_of_items: generated from templates filled with crowd-sourced object-attribute labels (pp.2-4)
instances: generated (template filling; 160K pre-generated, and the pipeline can produce more, pp.1-3)
evaluation: multiple choice and Boolean: agreement with the majority human response weighted by inter-annotator agreement (Track 1), accuracy (Tracks 2 and 3) (p.5)
human_validation: 20,000+ crowd-sourced annotations, at least four per object-attribute pair, kept only at 0.75 agreement (3 of 4) and only for extreme ratings (pp.2-3); human agreement reported as a reference in Table 4 (p.6). No validation of individual generated questions is reported; the authors note crowdsourcing may introduce errors (p.9).

engtrace_use.sentence: S-P1 (L172-177): '... others target advanced symbolic (Zhang et al., 2025b; Qiu et al., 2025) or qualitative (Wang et al., 2023; Shojaee et al., 2025) understanding.' S-P2 (L177-180, uncited, covers all six): 'Despite this progress, these benchmarks remain confined to theoretical physics, lacking the integrative context of engineering.'
engtrace_use.explanation: S-P1 alone is accurate for NEWTON: it tests qualitative understanding of physical attributes (low/moderate/high ratings, multiple-choice and Boolean questions, pp.2-4). S-P2 is wrong for it: NEWTON is about everyday household objects and practical scenarios (packing a backpack, hammering a nail, a sorting robot; p.4), motivated by robotic manipulation (p.1), the opposite of theoretical physics. Taken together, the paragraph presents NEWTON as a theoretical-physics benchmark, which the paper does not support. The May text also omits that NEWTON generates its questions from templates (pp.1-3), which bears on EngTrace's presentation of symbolic templates as its generative mechanism (L84-94).

suggested_wording: NEWTON (Wang et al., 2023) fills question templates with crowd-sourced attributes of everyday objects to generate multiple-choice questions on qualitative physical reasoning.
facts_to_cite: Repository of 2,800 object-attribute pairs (700+ everyday objects, 8 physical attributes) from 20,000+ crowd-sourced annotations, at least four per pair, filtered at 0.75 agreement (pp.1-3)

Questions are generated by filling templates from the repository; the benchmark has 160K questions in three tracks (comprehension, explicit application, implicit scenario analysis), and the pipeline can generate more (pp.1-4)
Questions are multiple choice or Boolean (p.4), scored by agreement with the human majority or by accuracy (p.5)
GPT-4 is less consistent than humans on object-attribute reasoning (50% vs 84%) (p.1)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: generated instances from templates (pp.1-3); human labels with an agreement filter (p.3). Lacks: quantitative problem solving (all questions are multiple choice or Boolean about qualitative attributes, p.4); gold traces; step-level evaluation; an engineering domain (everyday objects); any validation of an evaluator beyond the human label agreement. Its templates vary which objects fill a slot, not numerical parameters of a solved problem.
notes: The verdict combines an accurate S-P1 with an S-P2 that is wrong for this paper; a reviewer weighing only the citing sentence S-P1 would say accurate. NEWTON is the most peripheral of the six to EngTrace and the first to cut if space is short; if kept, it is the honest place to acknowledge that template-generated questions predate EngTrace in physical reasoning. Naming clash: in the May reference list 'Wang et al., 2023' is NEWTON, while the July rebuttal used 'Wang et al., 2023' for SciBench; if SciBench is added, cite it from ICML 2024 or disambiguate. Minor reference error: 'Jia Duan' should be Jiafei Duan (p.1); update the entry to Findings of EMNLP 2023 if the venue is confirmed.
